stat-u3-t1-001: A probability describes what happens over many repetitions, not in a few shots.
“Exactly 3 of every 4” and “makes the next three” claim short-run certainty, which probability never gives.
stat-u3-t1-002: The law of large numbers is about the proportion of heads, not the count.
Heads never becomes “due,” and the proportion need not be exactly 0.5 at any fixed number of tosses.
stat-u3-t1-004: A make should have probability 0.7, so 7 of the 10 digits must stand for a make.
“1–7 make, 7–9 miss” uses 7 twice, and “0–7” gives 8 digits (0.8).
stat-u3-t1-005: A simulated proportion varies by chance; its accuracy depends on the number of trials.
Rounding, changing the die or reusing the same digits does not get closer to the true value.
stat-u3-t1-015: The events are not mutually exclusive (28 juniors have pets), and overlap alone does not show independence.
stat-u3-t2-017: Without replacement, each draw changes the population slightly, so trials are not exactly independent.
Here n = 10 and 10% of N is 200, so 10 ≤ 200 and the binomial model is a good approximation.
stat-u3-t3-001: Ask whether the number describes every member of a population or only a sample.
One bag, 30 responses and 25 times are samples, so those are statistics; all candies from the factory is the population.
stat-u3-t3-002: Imagine taking every possible sample of the same size and computing p̂ for each one.
It is not the population or one sample’s values; it is the distribution of the statistic p̂.
stat-u3-t3-003: Bias is about the center of the sampling distribution.
Small spread and large samples describe variability, not bias, and no statistic always equals the parameter.
stat-u3-t3-004: Both dotplots are centered near 0.45, so neither statistic is biased.
The n = 100 dotplot is narrower, so larger samples vary less; the population proportion did not change.
stat-u3-t3-006: The CLT describes the sampling distribution of x̄ over many samples.
The population and the data in one sample keep their own shape, and x̄ still varies around μ.
stat-u3-t3-009: A t distribution replaces σ with s, which adds variability.
So it is symmetric about 0 with heavier tails, and it changes with the degrees of freedom.
stat-u3-s01-cp2-x01: Read a probability as a long-run relative frequency.
It does not describe the area covered or the hours of rain, and 30% does not mean “no rain.”
stat-u3-s01-cp2-x04: Six rolls is a short run, so three 4s is not surprising for a fair die.
Dice have no memory, so the next roll still has probability 1/6 of showing a 4.
stat-u3-s01-cp2-x05: A probability of 0.02 is close to 0 but not equal to 0.
So the event is rare but possible: about 2 in 100 in the long run, not exactly 2 in every 100.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x01: Ten tosses vary a lot, so 0.7 is weak evidence; the larger run gives the better estimate.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x02: The gambler’s fallacy is believing a streak makes the opposite result more likely.
Believing a win is “due” after five losses is exactly that mistake.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x03: Each hospital has a long-run proportion of boys near 0.5.
With only 15 births a day, the daily proportion swings more, so it passes 60% more often.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x04: The actual count varies from group to group, so 5 is an average, not a guarantee.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x05: The law of large numbers: over many trials, the proportion settles near the true probability.
It does not make heads “due” after tails, and it does not give exactly 50 heads in 100 tosses.
stat-u3-s01-honors-x01: Now 520/1,000 = 0.52. Over many more tosses, new results swamp the early excess.

stat-u3-s01-honors-x02: Each policy is a trial with a small claim probability.
With 100,000 independent policies, the overall claim rate is very close to that probability.
stat-u3-s01-honors-x03: The actual number of 6s varies around 10 from one set of 60 rolls to the next.
stat-u3-s02-cp2-x05: Mutually exclusive means P(A and B) = 0.

stat-u3-s02-honors-x03: Mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0. Independent: P(B | A) = P(B).
If A occurs, a disjoint B cannot, so they are dependent, not the same idea.
stat-u3-s03-cp2-x03: Read P(A | B) as “the probability of A given B.”
It is not P(A and B) or P(A or B); it restricts attention to the cases where B happened.
stat-u3-s03-cp2-x06: Independence means one event gives no information about the other.
“Cannot happen together” and P(A and B) = 0 describe mutually exclusive events, not independent ones.
stat-u3-s03-cp1-x04: Look for two events produced by separate, unrelated chance processes.
A coin and a die cannot affect each other, so those events are independent.
stat-u3-s03-honors-x02: Write P(A and B) two ways using the multiplication rule.
P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different, so only the product form is always true.
stat-u3-s04-cp2-x01: A make needs probability 0.8, so 8 of the 10 digits stand for a make.
0–8 is 9 digits (0.9), 1–8 leaves 9 unassigned, and even digits give 0.5.
stat-u3-s04-cp2-x02: Some chance processes are too complicated to find probabilities by formula.
Repeating the process many times gives a relative frequency that estimates the probability.
stat-u3-s04-cp2-x03: An estimate from only 50 trials varies a lot by chance.
Reusing numbers or changing the model does not help; more trials make it more reliable.
stat-u3-s04-cp2-x04: Each of the six faces must get the same number of digits.
Using 1–6 and skipping the other digits keeps each face at probability 1/6.
stat-u3-s04-cp1-x01: One trial must copy the whole process: buy boxes until every toy has been collected.
Record the number of boxes needed; stopping at a single 4 or after four draws is a different process.
stat-u3-s04-cp1-x02: A simulation is only as good as how well it matches the real process.
If the real outcomes are independent, the random numbers must be independent too.
stat-u3-s04-cp1-x03: It is an estimate: the next 1,000 trials will not give exactly 23.
stat-u3-s04-honors-x02: Both runs estimate the same probability.
The 10,000-trial estimate varies much less, so it is likely closer to the true value.
stat-u3-s04-honors-x03: Even and odd digits each have probability 0.5.
So the model assumes boys and girls are equally likely and one child does not affect the next.
stat-u3-s05-cp2-x05: A discrete random variable has values you can list, often counts.
Weight, height and time are measured on a continuous scale.
stat-u3-s05-cp1-x06: A discrete distribution lists each value with its probability.
It does not have to be symmetric, and the probabilities do not have to be equal.
stat-u3-s06-cp2-x04: E(X) is the mean of the probability distribution.
Read it as the long-run average over many games, not a score in any one game.
stat-u3-s07-cp2-x06: Check the BINS conditions for a binomial setting.
The number of trials must be fixed, and success does not have to be more likely than failure.
stat-u3-s07-cp1-x04: After a heart is dealt, fewer hearts remain, so P(heart) changes.

stat-u3-s08-cp2-x05: For independent X and Y, the variances add.
Standard deviations do not add, so find the variance first, then take the square root.
stat-u3-s08-cp2-x06: Means: μ_(X ± Y) = μ_X ± μ_Y. Independent variances: σ²_(X ± Y) = σ²_X + σ²_Y.
Variances add even for a difference, and SDs never add directly.
stat-u3-s08-honors-x02: Adding variances is valid only when X and Y are independent.

stat-u3-s09-cp2-x03: Imagine every possible sample of the same size and the statistic from each one.
One sample’s data or the population distribution is not a sampling distribution.
stat-u3-s09-cp2-x05: A parameter describes the whole population or process; a statistic comes from a sample.
So 41.2 hours (80 batteries) is x̄, and 40 hours (the process) is μ.
stat-u3-s09-cp1-x04: The SD formula assumes observations are independent.
Sampling without replacement is close to independent only when n ≤ 10% of N.
stat-u3-s09-honors-x03: σ_p̂ = √(p(1 − p)/n), so the SD is divided by √n.
Multiplying n by 4 divides the SD by √4 = 2.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x01: Larger samples contain more information about the population.
So statistics vary less from sample to sample; bias does not change with n.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x02: Unbiased describes where the sampling distribution is centered.
A small spread or a large sample is about variability, not bias.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x03: Spread of the darts shows variability; distance from the bullseye shows bias.
Tight grouping away from the center is low variability with high bias.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x04: The CLT is about the sampling distribution of x̄.
Individual samples and the population keep their own shapes.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x05: The spread of x̄ is σ/√n.
Only a larger n shrinks it; population size and a biased method do not.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x07: The mean of the sampling distribution of x̄ is μ, and its SD is σ/√n.
x̄ varies from sample to sample, so it does not always equal μ, and n does not create bias.
stat-u3-s10-cp1-x02: The CLT applies to the mean of a large random sample.
One income, 100 individual incomes, and the mean of only 3 incomes stay skewed right.
stat-u3-s10-honors-x01: A sample cannot contain values outside the population, so its range is at most the population range.
It is usually smaller, so its sampling distribution is centered below the true range.
stat-u3-s10-honors-x02: So both SDs are √(0.4 × 0.6/500) ≈ 0.022, approximately equal.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x06: Twelve reviews is a very small number of trials.

stat-u3-s01-honors-x06: Each weekly draw is independent of the past.
Twenty years of losses do not change next week’s probability of 1/1,000,000.
stat-u3-s01-honors-x07: Read a probability as a long-run proportion of many similar cars.
It is not “exactly 8 of every 100” and not part of a year or part of a car.
stat-u3-s03-cp1-x05: Compare P(GPA > 3.5) for students with and without a job.
0.30 ≠ 0.45, so knowing about a job changes the probability: not independent.
stat-u3-s04-cp1-x06: Simulated averages vary around the true mean by chance.
6.3 is close to 6 for 100 trials; more trials would likely bring it closer.
stat-u3-s04-honors-x05: The usual simulation picks a random integer from 1 to 365 for each person.

stat-u3-s04-honors-x07: Treat the simulated proportion like p̂ with n = 50.

stat-u3-s05-honors-x07: Discrete variables count; continuous variables measure.
Buses, passengers and stops are counts; exact time is a measurement.
stat-u3-s08-honors-x04: X + X = 2X, and a variable is completely dependent on itself.
Multiplying by 2 multiplies the SD by 2: SD(2X) = 6, not √18.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x08: An unbiased estimator has a sampling distribution centered at the parameter.
The mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ is p.
stat-u3-s10-cp1-x04: Bias comes from how the sample is chosen; variability depends on n.
A larger sample from the same biased frame still misses the same people.
stat-u3-s01-cp2-x12: A rare but possible event has a small positive probability, not 0.
stat-u3-s01-cp1-x13: The law of large numbers: averages over many trials become stable.

stat-u3-s01-honors-x16: The law of large numbers describes long-run proportions of independent trials.

stat-u3-s03-cp2-x15: The event after the bar is what we know happened: here, A.
stat-u3-s04-cp2-x13: Heads needs probability 0.5, so 5 of the 10 digits.

stat-u3-s04-cp2-x15: A simulation repeats a model of the random process many times.

stat-u3-s04-cp2-x18: Real repetitions of the process do not affect each other.

stat-u3-s04-cp1-x15: Two runs of the same simulation use different random numbers.

stat-u3-s05-cp1-x17: Continuous variables are measured and can take any value in an interval.

stat-u3-s06-cp2-x13: E(X) is the mean of the random variable’s probability distribution.

stat-u3-s07-cp2-x13: X counts the trials until the first success; it has no fixed number of trials.

stat-u3-s08-honors-x14: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) holds only when X and Y are independent.

stat-u3-s09-honors-x13: n = 400 is more than 200, so the formula overstates the SD.
stat-u3-s10-cp2-x13: An estimator is unbiased when its sampling distribution centers on the true value.

stat-u3-s10-cp2-x15: A biased method gives estimates that are systematically too high or too low.

stat-u3-s10-cp2-x16: Variability is the spread of the sampling distribution.

stat-u3-s10-cp1-x10: An unbiased estimator of μ has a sampling distribution centered at μ.

stat-u3-s10-cp1-x11: The CLT is about sample means over many samples.

stat-u3-s10-honors-x12: The CLT needs a large n to make x̄ approximately Normal.

stat-u3-s10-honors-x13: Bias depends on how units are selected; variability depends on n.
